title: Pentagon, Raytheon Sign Up to $6.3 Billion Multi-Year Deal for SM-3 IB Missiles
summary: The Pentagon and Raytheon have signed a multi-year contract worth up to $6.3 billion for SM-3 Block IB interceptors, months after a framework deal to raise production.
content:
The Pentagon has signed a multi-year contract with Raytheon worth up to $6.3 billion for SM-3 Block IB interceptors, locking in long-term production of one of the Navy's most important missile-defense weapons.

The deal, reported by Breaking Defense, lands just months after the Defense Department and Raytheon inked a framework agreement aimed at boosting output of the air-defense munition. Multi-year contracts of this kind let the Pentagon order at steadier, higher rates while giving industry the confidence to invest in its own production lines.

The SM-3 Block IB is the backbone of sea-based ballistic missile defense. Fired from Aegis-equipped destroyers and cruisers — and from the Aegis Ashore sites in Europe — it intercepts short- to intermediate-range ballistic missiles outside the atmosphere, using a kinetic warhead that destroys its target by collision rather than explosives.

Demand for interceptors has climbed sharply in recent years. U.S. warships have expended SM-series missiles in real combat defending against missile and drone attacks in the Middle East, and replenishing those magazines has become a stated priority for Navy leadership.

Neither the Pentagon nor Raytheon has disclosed the exact number of missiles covered or the delivery schedule. As with most large munitions contracts, the ceiling value represents the maximum the government can order over the life of the agreement.
imageAlt: Pentagon, Raytheon Sign Up to $6.3 Billion Multi-Year Deal for SM-3 IB Missiles
author: James Carter

title: Boeing Wins F/A-XX Contract for Navy's Next-Generation Stealth Fighter
summary: Boeing has won the F/A-XX contract to build the Navy's next-generation carrier-based stealth fighter, one of the most anticipated awards in years.
content:
Boeing has won the competition to build the F/A-XX, the Navy's next-generation stealth fighter that will eventually replace the F/A-18 Super Hornet aboard U.S. aircraft carriers.

The award, reported by The War Zone, ends months of uncertainty around a program the Pentagon had at one point tried to freeze. F/A-XX has been among the most closely watched contract decisions in military aviation, with the future of naval air power hanging on its outcome.

The new fighter is expected to fly farther, carry more weapons, and operate alongside uncrewed "loyal wingman" drones as part of the Navy's Next Generation Air Dominance family of systems. It will form the manned centerpiece of the carrier air wing of the 2030s, working with the MQ-25 Stingray tanker drone and a growing fleet of collaborative combat aircraft.

For Boeing's defense business, the win is a major reversal of fortune. The company's fighter portfolio had been thinning as F/A-18 production winds down, and losing F/A-XX would have effectively ended Boeing as a builder of manned tactical fighters.

The Navy has not yet released the contract value or a first-flight timeline. Expect those details — and the losing bidders' next moves — to emerge in the coming weeks.
imageAlt: Boeing Wins F/A-XX Contract for Navy's Next-Generation Stealth Fighter
author: Michael Reynolds

title: Taiwan's First F-16 Block 70 Fighters Finally Arrive
summary: Taiwan has taken delivery of its first two new F-16 Block 70 fighters, kicking off a long-awaited fleet expansion as pressure from mainland China grows.
content:
Taiwan has received its first two F-16 Block 70 fighters, the long-delayed start of a major expansion of the island's fighter fleet.

The delivery, reported by The War Zone, begins the fulfillment of an order placed years ago that has been repeatedly pushed back. For Taipei, the new jets — the most advanced F-16 variant ever built, with an AESA radar and modern avionics — are a badly needed reinforcement.

Taiwan's air force flies one of the oldest fighter fleets in the region, and its pilots scramble constantly to shadow Chinese military aircraft operating around the island. Beijing has steadily increased the scale and intensity of those operations, and Taiwanese defense planners have warned that the airframes they have are wearing out under the tempo.

The Block 70s, often called the F-16V, bring Taiwan's Vipers close to fifth-generation standards in sensors and networking, even without stealth. They will join an ongoing upgrade of Taiwan's existing F-16A/B fleet to a similar standard.

Further deliveries are expected to continue over the coming years, though the exact pace has not been made public.
imageAlt: Taiwan's First F-16 Block 70 Fighters Finally Arrive
author: David Sullivan

title: USAF's New HACM Hypersonic Cruise Missile Makes First Release Over Australian Range
summary: The U.S. Air Force has carried out the first release of its Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile over an Australian test range, a milestone after major program delays.
content:
The U.S. Air Force has conducted the first release of its new Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile (HACM) over a test range in Australia, putting the long-delayed weapon into flight testing at last.

The test, reported by The War Zone, is a joint U.S.-Australian effort. Australia's vast, sparsely populated test ranges have become the proving ground of choice for Western hypersonic programs, offering the long flight corridors the weapons need.

HACM is an air-breathing hypersonic cruise missile, designed to fly at more than five times the speed of sound while maneuvering in the atmosphere — a combination that makes it extremely hard to intercept. It is meant to give bombers and fighters a conventional strike weapon that can penetrate defended airspace.

The program has suffered major delays, and the successful release marks a turning point. The Pentagon is racing to field operational hypersonic weapons as China and Russia deploy their own, and flight-test data from HACM will feed directly into follow-on designs.

Neither the Air Force nor its Australian partners has released details of the test outcome.
imageAlt: USAF's New HACM Hypersonic Cruise Missile Makes First Release Over Australian Range
author: Robert Hayes

title: Anduril and U.S. Navy Announce $6.6 Billion Push to Expand Submarine Industrial Base
summary: Anduril Industries and the U.S. Navy are investing a combined $6.6 billion to expand America's submarine industrial base, anchored by a new software-defined shipyard.
content:
Anduril Industries and the U.S. Navy are putting a combined $6.6 billion into expanding America's submarine industrial base, in one of the largest private-public shipbuilding investments in decades.

The centerpiece, announced October 6, is Arsenal-2, a new software-defined shipyard backed by a $3.7 billion private capital investment from Anduril. The facility will manufacture critical components for the Virginia-class attack submarine, adding badly needed capacity to a strained supply chain, according to Naval News.

U.S. submarine production has been the pacing problem for naval planners for years. The Navy wants to build two Virginia-class boats a year while simultaneously starting the Columbia-class ballistic missile submarine — a workload the current industrial base has struggled to meet, with suppliers stretched thin and skilled labor in short supply.

Anduril, best known for drones and autonomous systems, is now moving directly into heavy manufacturing. A software-defined shipyard implies heavy automation, digital design tools, and production methods borrowed from the tech industry rather than traditional shipbuilding.

If it works, the model could reshape how America builds warships. If it stumbles, the submarine programs it is meant to rescue will feel it first.
imageAlt: Anduril and U.S. Navy Announce $6.6 Billion Push to Expand Submarine Industrial Base
author: James Carter

title: Navy Orders 30 Drone Ships in Big Push for Medium Uncrewed Vessels
summary: The U.S. Navy has ordered 30 medium uncrewed surface vessels, a major step toward fielding larger drone ship fleets after years of struggle.
content:
The U.S. Navy has ordered 30 medium uncrewed surface vessels, taking what The War Zone calls an important step toward fielding larger fleets of drone ships.

The order targets the "medium" USV category — vessels big enough to carry meaningful sensors and weapons over long distances, but small and cheap enough to buy in numbers and risk in contested waters. It is an area where the Navy has, by its own admission, persistently struggled to move from experiments to real capability.

Uncrewed vessels are central to the Navy's vision of a future "hybrid fleet," in which relatively small numbers of large manned warships are multiplied by scores of robotic ones handling surveillance, mine warfare, electronic warfare, and even missile strikes.

Past efforts stumbled on reliability, autonomy, and murky requirements. This order suggests the Navy believes the technology — and its own concept for using it — has matured enough to commit real money.

Details on the winning design, unit cost, and delivery timeline have not been disclosed.
imageAlt: Navy Orders 30 Drone Ships in Big Push for Medium Uncrewed Vessels
author: Michael Reynolds

title: Sweden Launches First Patriot Air Defense Mission to Poland
summary: Sweden has launched its first Patriot air defense mission to Poland as part of a NATO operation, amid a heated domestic security debate.
content:
Sweden has launched its first Patriot air defense mission to Poland, deploying the U.S.-made missile system abroad under a NATO mission for the first time.

The move, reported by Breaking Defense, comes at a politically charged moment in Stockholm, where a new government is taking power and security policy sits at the heart of a fierce political row. Sweden joined NATO only recently, and how far its forces should deploy in collective defense is still being contested at home.

Poland has become the alliance's front line for air defense. Positioned on NATO's eastern flank, it hosts a growing web of Patriot batteries, radars, and allied detachments meant to deter Russian missile and drone attacks — a threat made concrete by the war in Ukraine.

The Patriot system, built by Raytheon, is the alliance's workhorse for intercepting ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and aircraft. Sweden's deployment adds another layer to Poland's coverage and signals Stockholm's willingness to put hardware behind its NATO commitments.

Neither government has disclosed the size of the Swedish contingent or how long the mission will last.
imageAlt: Sweden Launches First Patriot Air Defense Mission to Poland
author: David Sullivan

title: Pentagon, Lockheed Weigh Multi-Year F-35 Production and Sustainment Deal
summary: The Pentagon and Lockheed Martin are negotiating a multi-year F-35 production and sustainment agreement, though doubts remain over long-term cost savings.
content:
The Pentagon and Lockheed Martin are negotiating a multi-year agreement covering F-35 production and sustainment, a deal that could reshape the economics of the world's largest fighter program.

The talks, first reported by Breaking Defense, would bundle several years of aircraft buys and long-term support into a single contract — the kind of arrangement the Pentagon favors for driving down unit costs through stable, predictable orders.

But skepticism is already surfacing. One source familiar with the negotiations expressed doubt that Lockheed "can successfully propose something that demonstrates long-term cost savings," a pointed reminder that the F-35's sustainment bill — the cost of keeping the fleet flying — has been the program's most stubborn problem for a decade.

With more than 1,000 F-35s delivered worldwide and production still running, even small percentage shifts in sustainment costs translate into tens of billions of dollars over the fleet's lifetime. That is what makes these negotiations some of the highest-stakes contracting in the defense world.

No timeline for an agreement has been announced.
imageAlt: Pentagon, Lockheed Weigh Multi-Year F-35 Production and Sustainment Deal
author: Robert Hayes

title: GDLS to Deliver New PERCH 2.0 Loitering Munition Prototypes to Army This Month
summary: General Dynamics Land Systems will deliver four PERCH 2.0 loitering munition prototypes to the Army's 1st Cavalry Division by the end of October.
content:
General Dynamics Land Systems is set to deliver four prototypes of its new PERCH 2.0 loitering munition platform to the Army by the end of October, putting fresh hardware into soldiers' hands within weeks.

The prototypes are headed to the 1st Brigade, 1st Cavalry Division under an existing contract, a company executive told Breaking Defense. Getting early versions to an operational brigade lets the Army test the system the way it would actually be used — and feed fixes back before larger buys.

Loitering munitions — essentially one-way attack drones that circle over the battlefield until they find a target — have become one of the most consequential weapons of the Ukraine war. Both sides have used them by the thousands against armor, artillery, and air defenses, and every major army is now racing to field its own.

PERCH 2.0 is GDLS's bid for a slice of that demand from the U.S. Army, which has been moving urgently to equip brigades with organic drone strike capability rather than relying solely on higher-echelon assets.

The company has not disclosed the munition's range, warhead size, or unit cost.
imageAlt: GDLS to Deliver New PERCH 2.0 Loitering Munition Prototypes to Army This Month
author: James Carter

title: Australia Receives Second HIMARS Tranche Two Years Ahead of Schedule
summary: The Australian Army has received a second tranche of U.S.-built HIMARS rocket launchers, arriving two years ahead of schedule.
content:
The Australian Army has taken delivery of a second tranche of High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS) launchers from the United States — two years ahead of schedule.

The early arrival, reported by Army Technology, is a notable bright spot in a defense procurement landscape more often defined by delays. For Australia, which is reorienting its military toward long-range strike in the Indo-Pacific, HIMARS is a centerpiece capability.

The truck-mounted system became famous in Ukraine, where its precision rockets devastated Russian ammunition depots and command posts far behind the front lines. Australia wants the same reach: the ability to strike targets at long distance from mobile, hard-to-find launchers.

Canberra's accelerated delivery suggests both strong U.S.-Australian industrial coordination and the priority Washington places on arming allies in the region. Further tranches are expected as Australia builds out its long-range fires enterprise, including domestic missile production efforts.

The Army has not said how many launchers were in this tranche.
imageAlt: Australia Receives Second HIMARS Tranche Two Years Ahead of Schedule
author: Michael Reynolds

title: Could Germany Join GCAP? UK Seeks to Advance Potential Fighter Switch
summary: Britain is pushing to advance talks on Germany potentially joining the GCAP sixth-generation fighter program after the collapse of FCAS.
content:
Britain is seeking to "progress" talks that could bring Germany into the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP), the sixth-generation fighter project it leads with Japan and Italy.

The outreach, reported by Breaking Defense, follows the collapse of the Franco-German-Spanish FCAS program this summer — a breakup that left Berlin hunting for a next-generation fighter path and threw Europe's combat air plans into disarray.

GCAP aims to field a crewed sixth-generation fighter in the 2030s, built around stealth, long range, and manned-unmanned teaming with drone wingmen. Adding Germany — Europe's largest defense spender — would bring money, industrial weight, and political heft, but also new complications over workshare and requirements.

For London, German participation would validate GCAP as the European alternative after FCAS fell apart. For Berlin, it is one of several options on the table, alongside potential American offerings.

No formal negotiations have been announced, and officials on both sides are characterizing the contacts as exploratory.
imageAlt: Could Germany Join GCAP? UK Seeks to Advance Potential Fighter Switch
author: David Sullivan

title: Arizona Desert Drone Tests Offer Hard Lessons for CENTCOM's Counter-UAS Fight
summary: Counter-drone experiments in the Arizona desert are shaping how U.S. forces in the Middle East confront the drone threat.
content:
Counter-drone experiments in the Arizona desert are delivering hard lessons for U.S. Central Command, where American forces face one of the world's most intense drone threats.

Officials say the "realities of the desert" — intense heat, wind, dust, and glare — closely replicate the physical challenges troops confront across the Middle East, Breaking Defense reports. If a sensor, jammer, or interceptor works at Yuma, the thinking goes, it has a far better chance of working in Iraq or Syria.

The threat is no longer theoretical. Iranian-backed groups have repeatedly attacked U.S. bases with one-way attack drones, and defending against them has consumed expensive interceptors and strained air defenses. Cheap drones versus costly defenses is the defining cost-exchange problem of the current fight.

The Arizona trials put counter-UAS systems through realistic conditions: cluttered skies, degraded sensors, and operators under pressure. What fails there gets fixed before it is asked to protect troops downrange.

The work feeds directly into CENTCOM's defenses, where commanders have made counter-drone capability one of their most urgent requests.
imageAlt: Arizona Desert Drone Tests Offer Hard Lessons for CENTCOM's Counter-UAS Fight
author: Robert Hayes

title: New Leaders, New Drone Command: What to Expect from AUSA 2026
summary: The Army's autonomy push and the fate of its modernization programs will dominate this year's AUSA conference, with new leaders and a new drone command in the spotlight.
content:
The Association of the U.S. Army's annual conference opens with the service at an inflection point: new leaders at the top, a new drone command standing up, and big questions about which modernization programs survive.

The Army's autonomy push will loom largest, Breaking Defense reports. After watching drones reshape the war in Ukraine, the service is reorganizing how it buys, fields, and fights with uncrewed systems — and standing up dedicated formations to do it.

Also under the microscope: the future of the Army's marquee modernization programs. With budgets under pressure and priorities shifting toward drones, long-range fires, and air defense, some legacy efforts face hard scrutiny from the new leadership.

Industry will be listening closely. AUSA is where the Army signals, often bluntly, what it wants to buy — and just as importantly, what it no longer wants. Expect contract announcements, prototype unveilings, and carefully worded warnings to programs falling behind.

Defense News will be covering the conference's major developments as they happen.
imageAlt: New Leaders, New Drone Command: What to Expect from AUSA 2026
author: James Carter

title: USCYBERCOM Wraps 13th Annual Cyber Flag Exercise with Global Partners
summary: U.S. Cyber Command has concluded its 13th annual Cyber Flag exercise after nearly three weeks of simulated cyber combat alongside global partners.
content:
U.S. Cyber Command has concluded its 13th annual Cyber Flag exercise, wrapping nearly three weeks of intense, simulated cyber combat alongside partners and allies from around the world.

The exercise, held in Suffolk, Virginia, ended July 31, 2026, according to the Defense Department. Teams faced simulated malicious cyber threats designed to test their ability to defend military networks under realistic, high-pressure conditions.

Cyber Flag has grown into the premier exercise for the U.S. cyber mission force, bringing together operators from across the services and allied nations. This year's iteration also gathered senior military cyber leaders for a multi-national symposium on the sidelines — a sign of how central coalition cyber operations have become.

Real-world stakes back the training. State-linked hackers probe U.S. and allied networks daily, and exercises like Cyber Flag are where defenders rehearse the coordination those attacks demand — across agencies, services, and borders.

Cyber Command has not released details of the scenarios used, citing operational security.
imageAlt: USCYBERCOM Wraps 13th Annual Cyber Flag Exercise with Global Partners
author: Michael Reynolds

title: Zero Trust Gets Harder as Every Weapon and AI Agent Needs an Identity
summary: The Pentagon's Zero Trust push is entering a harder phase: giving every user, device, weapon system, and AI agent its own verifiable identity.
content:
The Pentagon's Zero Trust cybersecurity drive is entering its hardest phase yet — extending identity-based security beyond people and laptops to every weapon system, sensor, and AI agent on the network.

That was the takeaway from a Breaking Defense webinar, where experts described the next stage of the effort: in a future force where drones, autonomous vehicles, and AI software all act on data, each one needs a verifiable identity before it can be trusted.

Zero Trust assumes no user or device is trustworthy by default, verifying every access request. Applying that to weapons is a different order of difficulty. A fighter jet, a missile battery, or an AI targeting assistant cannot simply be issued a password — their identities must be baked into hardware and software, resilient to jamming, spoofing, and capture.

The stakes are rising as the military networks more of its arsenal together. A single compromised node in a connected force could poison targeting data or blind commanders — which is exactly what adversaries are trying to achieve.

Officials say the identity problem is now one of the pacing challenges for the Pentagon's broader digital modernization.
imageAlt: Zero Trust Gets Harder as Every Weapon and AI Agent Needs an Identity
author: David Sullivan

title: Navy Commissions Destroyer USS Ted Stevens in Alaska Ceremony
summary: The Navy has commissioned its newest destroyer, USS Ted Stevens, into active service during a ceremony in Whittier, Alaska.
content:
The Navy has commissioned its newest guided-missile destroyer, the USS Ted Stevens, into active service during a formal ceremony in Whittier, Alaska.

The ship honors the late Alaska senator Ted Stevens, a longtime advocate for defense spending and Arctic security whose name now sails on one of the fleet's most capable surface combatants, according to the Defense Department.

As an Arleigh Burke-class Flight III destroyer, the Ted Stevens carries the SPY-6 radar — a major leap in sensitivity over earlier ships — and the Aegis combat system that anchors U.S. naval air and missile defense. Flight III hulls are the Navy's answer to increasingly sophisticated missile threats.

Basing the commissioning in Alaska was itself a statement. The Arctic is becoming a zone of strategic competition, and the Navy has been working to prove it can operate its most advanced ships in the region's harsh conditions.

The Ted Stevens now joins the Pacific Fleet, where demand for missile-defense-capable destroyers continues to outstrip supply.
imageAlt: Navy Commissions Destroyer USS Ted Stevens in Alaska Ceremony
author: Robert Hayes

title: Air Force Names Its New Drone Wingmen: FQ-42 Vengeance and FQ-44 Fury
summary: The Air Force has officially named its first Collaborative Combat Aircraft the FQ-42 Vengeance and FQ-44 Fury.
content:
The U.S. Air Force has given names to its future drone wingmen. The service's first two Collaborative Combat Aircraft designs will be called the FQ-42 Vengeance and the FQ-44 Fury, Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink announced during a keynote at the Air and Space Forces Association's Air, Space and Cyber Conference on Sept. 14.

The naming is more than ceremony. It signals that the CCA program — the Air Force's effort to field thousands of AI-piloted drones that fly alongside crewed fighters — is moving from concept to real hardware with real designations.

CCAs are designed to be affordable, attritable unmanned aircraft that extend the reach of fighters like the F-35 and the future F-47. They can carry sensors and weapons deep into contested airspace, scout ahead, jam enemy radars, or strike targets — missions too dangerous or too numerous for manned jets alone.

The "FQ" designation follows Air Force convention: F for fighter, Q for unmanned. Two named designs suggest at least two vendors' aircraft are maturing in parallel, keeping competition alive as the program scales.

The Air Force has said it wants the first CCAs operational before the end of the decade, with the fleet eventually numbering in the thousands.
imageAlt: Air Force Names Its New Drone Wingmen: FQ-42 Vengeance and FQ-44 Fury
author: James Carter

title: NORAD F-16s Deploy to the High North for Operation Arctic Vanguard
summary: F-16s from Eielson Air Force Base have deployed to Goose Bay, Canada, for Arctic defense missions under Operation Arctic Vanguard.
content:
F-16 Fighting Falcons from Eielson Air Force Base, Alaska, have deployed to Goose Bay in Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada, to fly defense missions across the Arctic under Operation Arctic Vanguard.

The deployment, announced by the Alaskan NORAD Region, puts American fighters at a forward Canadian base covering the northern approaches to North America — the flight path Russian long-range bombers and cruise missiles would take in a conflict.

The Arctic has become a growing security concern. Russia has reopened Cold War-era bases along its northern coast, and China has declared itself a "near-Arctic state" while expanding its icebreaker fleet. NORAD, the joint U.S.-Canadian command, is responsible for detecting and intercepting threats in the region.

The F-16s at Eielson belong to the Air Force's Pacific air forces and are no strangers to Arctic operations, routinely training in extreme cold. Operating from Goose Bay extends their reach over the North Atlantic and eastern Arctic.

NORAD has not said how long the deployment will last or how many aircraft are involved.
imageAlt: NORAD F-16s Deploy to the High North for Operation Arctic Vanguard
author: Michael Reynolds

title: B-52 to Get Stealthy LRASM Anti-Ship Missiles, Completing the Bomber Trio
summary: The B-52 is being integrated with the stealthy AGM-158C LRASM, giving all three U.S. bombers a long-range anti-ship punch.
content:
The B-52 Stratofortress is getting the AGM-158C Long Range Anti-Ship Missile, completing the integration of the stealthy weapon across all three of America's heavy bombers.

With LRASM on the B-52, the B-1B, and the B-2 already able to carry it — and the future B-21 certain to follow — the Air Force can now hold enemy warships at risk from any of its bomber platforms, The War Zone reports.

LRASM is a subsonic, stealthy cruise missile designed to hunt ships autonomously in contested waters. Launched from hundreds of miles away, it uses onboard sensors to find and identify targets even when GPS and datalinks are jammed — exactly the conditions expected in a Pacific fight.

For the B-52, the pairing is potent. The 70-year-old bomber can carry a large load of cruise missiles and launch them from well outside enemy air defenses, turning it into what strategists call an "arsenal plane" for maritime strike.

The move reflects the Pentagon's focus on China, whose navy is now the world's largest by hull count. Sinking or deterring that fleet from long range is a central U.S. war plan.
imageAlt: B-52 to Get Stealthy LRASM Anti-Ship Missiles, Completing the Bomber Trio
author: David Sullivan

title: U.S. Pitches F-35 as Portugal Weighs Replacing Its F-16s
summary: Washington is making a hard push for the F-35 as Portugal decides what will replace its aging F-16 fleet.
content:
The United States is lobbying hard for Portugal to choose the F-35 Lightning II as the replacement for its aging F-16 fighters, as Lisbon weighs cost, capability, and strategic alignment.

Portugal's decision, reported by The War Zone, pits the American stealth fighter against European rivals. For a mid-size NATO air force, the choice is about more than jets — it determines decades of industrial partnerships, training pipelines, and interoperability.

The F-35's pitch is its sensor fusion and stealth, which have made it the default fifth-generation choice for most U.S. allies; more than a dozen countries now fly or have ordered it. European competitors counter with lower operating costs and promises of industrial workshare.

Portugal currently flies F-16AM/BM aircraft bought second-hand and upgraded years ago. Whatever Lisbon picks will anchor its airpower through the 2060s.

No decision timeline has been announced, but the American push suggests Washington sees the competition as genuinely contested.
imageAlt: U.S. Pitches F-35 as Portugal Weighs Replacing Its F-16s
author: Robert Hayes

title: Navy Doubles Down on X-BAT VTOL 'Fighter' Drone
summary: The Navy is accelerating the X-BAT, an ambitious vertical-takeoff drone meant to bring fighter-like capability to ships without catapults.
content:
The Navy is doubling down on the X-BAT, a vertical-takeoff-and-landing drone being developed to give fighter-like capability to ships that lack catapults and arresting gear.

Flight testing is approaching, and the program has laid out what The War Zone describes as an extremely ambitious timeline to reach operational capability. Shield AI, the autonomy company behind the design, has drawn major investment — reportedly reaching $400 million with U.S. government backing.

X-BAT's trick is its tail-sitter design: it takes off and lands vertically like a helicopter, then transitions to winged forward flight. That means it could operate from amphibious ships, destroyers, or expeditionary airfields — places no conventional fighter drone can go.

The Navy wants unmanned aircraft that can scout, strike, and jam from distributed ships across the Pacific. A VTOL fighter drone fits that vision precisely.

Ambitious timelines in drone development often slip. But the money flowing into X-BAT shows how seriously the Navy takes the concept.
imageAlt: Navy Doubles Down on X-BAT VTOL 'Fighter' Drone
author: James Carter

title: Army Shows 'Blackbeard' Hypersonic Missile Firing from Ground Launcher
summary: The Army has shown its Blackbeard hypersonic missile firing from a mobile ground launcher, part of a push for cheaper, more mobile hypersonic weapons.
content:
The U.S. Army has shown its Blackbeard hypersonic missile being fired from a mobile ground launcher, offering a rare public look at one of its newest strike programs.

Blackbeard is part of the Army's push to make hypersonic weapons more mobile and more affordable, The War Zone reports. Traditional hypersonic programs have been expensive and tied to large, fixed infrastructure; Blackbeard aims to put the capability on trucks that can hide, move, and shoot.

Hypersonic missiles fly at more than five times the speed of sound while maneuvering, compressing enemy reaction time to minutes. The Army wants them for striking high-value targets — air defenses, command posts, ships — deep inside contested territory.

A ground-launched hypersonic weapon also fills a gap left by decades of treaty limits. With those constraints gone, the Army is building a family of long-range fires from PrSM ballistic missiles up through hypersonics.

The footage does not reveal the missile's range or speed, and the Army has not announced a fielding date.
imageAlt: Army Shows 'Blackbeard' Hypersonic Missile Firing from Ground Launcher
author: Michael Reynolds

title: Where the Carriers Are: Bush Takes Liberty in Phuket, Washington Covers Iran
summary: USS George H.W. Bush pulled into Phuket after 188 days at sea, leaving USS George Washington as the sole carrier facing Iran.
content:
The USS George H.W. Bush has pulled into Phuket, Thailand, for its first liberty call after 188 days at sea — leaving the USS George Washington as the Navy's sole aircraft carrier supporting operations against Iran.

The snapshot, from The War Zone's regular carrier tracker, captures the strain on the fleet. With the Bush standing down after a grueling deployment, a single carrier is covering one of the world's most dangerous flashpoints.

Carrier deployments have been stretching longer as global demands pile up: deterring Iran, reassuring Pacific allies, and maintaining presence in the Mediterranean. The Navy has eleven carriers on paper, but maintenance backlogs mean far fewer are deployable at any given time.

The Bush's 188-day stretch at sea — more than six months — illustrates the tempo. Extended deployments wear on ships and sailors alike, and the Navy has acknowledged the pace is unsustainable.

The George Washington, forward-deployed to Japan, now carries the load in the Middle East alongside its escorts.
imageAlt: Where the Carriers Are: Bush Takes Liberty in Phuket, Washington Covers Iran
author: David Sullivan

title: First F-16 Block 72 Takes Flight, Seven Years After Morocco's Order
summary: The first F-16 Block 72 — the Pratt & Whitney-powered Viper ordered by Morocco seven years ago — has finally flown.
content:
The first F-16 Block 72 has taken to the air, seven years after Morocco became the launch customer for the variant.

The Block 72 is the latest evolution of the F-16, distinguished by its Pratt & Whitney F100 engine and the same advanced avionics as the Block 70: the APG-83 AESA radar, a modern glass cockpit, and the structural upgrades that extend the airframe's life to 12,000 hours.

Morocco's order kicked off the Block 72 line, and the long wait reflects both production ramp-up and the complexity of standing up a new variant. The flight marks the beginning of deliveries to Rabat, which is modernizing its air force amid regional tensions.

The F-16 production line in Greenville, South Carolina, now has a backlog stretching years into the future, with multiple countries waiting on new Vipers even as the design approaches its 50th anniversary.

For Lockheed Martin, every Block 70/72 delivery is proof the Viper remains commercially alive well into the stealth era.
imageAlt: First F-16 Block 72 Takes Flight, Seven Years After Morocco's Order
author: Robert Hayes

title: Northrop Grumman's Talon Blue Drone Takes Flight in CCA Race
summary: Northrop Grumman's Talon Blue has flown, staking its claim in the Air Force's Collaborative Combat Aircraft competition.
content:
Northrop Grumman's Talon Blue has taken flight, as the defense giant angles for a share of the Air Force's Collaborative Combat Aircraft portfolio.

The first flight, reported by The War Zone, puts Northrop's design in the air at a moment when the CCA program is accelerating. The Air Force wants potentially thousands of AI-piloted drones to fly alongside crewed fighters, and multiple vendors are competing to define what those aircraft look like.

Talon Blue's exact configuration remains closely held, but the CCA mission set is public: loyal-wingman drones that carry extra weapons, extend sensor coverage, jam enemy defenses, and take on the riskiest missions ahead of manned fighters.

Northrop, which builds the B-21 Raider stealth bomber, is betting its experience with advanced, survivable aircraft translates to the drone fight. It faces competition from General Atomics, Anduril, and others already flying CCA demonstrators.

With the Air Force now naming its first CCAs — the FQ-42 Vengeance and FQ-44 Fury — the race is shifting from viewgraphs to flying hardware.
imageAlt: Northrop Grumman's Talon Blue Drone Takes Flight in CCA Race
author: James Carter

title: B-1B Bombers Beat a Hasty Retreat from England Amid Iran Threats
summary: B-1B bombers have abruptly left RAF Fairford in England after Iran openly threatened the base that hosted them during Operation Epic Fury.
content:
B-1B Lancer bombers have made a hasty departure from RAF Fairford in England, after Iran openly threatened the base that hosted American bombers during Operation Epic Fury.

The sudden exit, reported by The War Zone, underscores how seriously the Pentagon takes Iranian threats against the facilities supporting its bomber operations. Some B-1s had remained at Fairford after the operation; the threats prompted a rapid dispersal.

The B-1B, America's supersonic conventional bomber, played a visible role in the strikes on Iran, flying long-range missions with heavy payloads of cruise missiles and guided bombs. Its presence in England was itself a signal — and Iran's threats were the response.

Dispersing bombers is standard practice when bases are threatened, but the speed of this move suggests the threat was considered credible and imminent.

The bombers' current location has not been disclosed.
imageAlt: B-1B Bombers Beat a Hasty Retreat from England Amid Iran Threats
author: Michael Reynolds

title: Coast Guard Orders Its First MQ-9B Drones in $248 Million Deal
summary: The U.S. Coast Guard has placed a $248 million order for its first MQ-9B drones to extend its maritime surveillance reach.
content:
The U.S. Coast Guard has placed a $248 million order for its first MQ-9B drones, bringing long-endurance unmanned surveillance to the maritime service.

The unarmed aircraft are meant to "give the Coast Guard crews a longer-range view of our maritime domain," a senior official said, according to Breaking Defense. The MQ-9B — the same family as the Air Force's Reaper — can stay airborne for more than 30 hours, scanning vast ocean areas for drug smugglers, illegal fishing, and distressed vessels.

For the Coast Guard, which patrols enormous areas with a small fleet of ships and aircraft, persistence is everything. A single drone can watch a smuggling corridor for a day and a half without refueling, cueing cutters to intercept.

The buy also reflects the MQ-9B's evolution into a multi-mission platform. Beyond the Coast Guard, variants serve with the Royal Air Force, and the Navy is eyeing carrier-based derivatives.

Deliveries and basing plans have not been announced.
imageAlt: Coast Guard Orders Its First MQ-9B Drones in $248 Million Deal
author: David Sullivan

title: Lockheed Unveils PAC-3 Edge, Its Next-Generation Patriot Interceptor
summary: Lockheed Martin has unveiled the PAC-3 Edge, a next-generation Patriot interceptor backed by hundreds of millions in company investment.
content:
Lockheed Martin has unveiled the PAC-3 Edge, its next-generation Patriot interceptor — and is putting hundreds of millions of dollars of its own money behind it.

The company plans to invest heavily in the missile itself, plus its seeker and solid rocket motor, Tim Cahill, president of Lockheed's missiles and fire control division, said, according to Breaking Defense. Company-funded development on this scale signals Lockheed's confidence in long-term demand.

The PAC-3 is the Patriot system's hit-to-kill interceptor, designed to destroy incoming ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and aircraft by slamming into them directly. It has seen real combat in the Middle East and Ukraine, where Patriot batteries have become among the most valuable — and most targeted — air defense assets in the world.

The "Edge" variant promises improved performance against evolving threats, including maneuvering hypersonic weapons that stress current interceptors.

With global demand for air defense at historic highs, Lockheed is betting the PAC-3 franchise has decades of growth ahead.
imageAlt: Lockheed Unveils PAC-3 Edge, Its Next-Generation Patriot Interceptor
author: Robert Hayes

title: Hanwha Eyes Army's Tracked Howitzer Program After Wheeled-Arty Win
summary: Hanwha plans to offer its K9 tracked howitzers for the Army's next artillery competition after winning the wheeled howitzer contest.
content:
South Korea's Hanwha is setting its sights on the U.S. Army's tracked howitzer program, planning to offer its K9A1 or K9A2 self-propelled guns for the competition.

A Hanwha executive told reporters of the plan, according to Breaking Defense — a move that follows the company's victory in the Army's wheeled howitzer competition. Winning both would make Hanwha the dominant foreign supplier of American artillery.

The K9 Thunder is one of the world's most successful artillery systems, in service with South Korea and exported to Poland, Norway, Finland, Australia, and others. The K9A2 variant adds automation, including an automatic loader that cuts crew size and raises the rate of fire.

The Army's artillery modernization has gained urgency from Ukraine, where massed tube artillery remains decisive. The service wants longer range, faster shooting, and guns that can move before counter-battery fire arrives.

Competition details and timelines have not been released.
imageAlt: Hanwha Eyes Army's Tracked Howitzer Program After Wheeled-Arty Win
author: James Carter

title: Army Lasers Blast Cartel Drones Out of the Sky in Border Test
summary: An Army high-energy laser has downed three hostile drones near the southern border, in a real-world proof of directed-energy weapons.
content:
An Army high-energy laser has shot down three hostile drones near the southern border, in one of the clearest real-world demonstrations yet of directed-energy weapons.

Service members assigned to Joint Task Force Southern Border used the Army's Multipurpose High Energy Laser to stop three unmanned aircraft deemed a threat, according to the Defense Department. The drones were believed linked to drug cartels using them for smuggling surveillance.

The engagement is a milestone for laser weapons, which have been "five years away" for decades. Unlike missile interceptors costing hundreds of thousands of dollars per shot, a laser kills for roughly the price of the diesel fuel running its generator — as long as it has power and a clear line of sight.

Cartel drones have become a genuine security problem, spotting for smugglers and probing border defenses. A weapon that can drop them cheaply and repeatedly changes the economics of that fight.

The Army did not say whether the laser will deploy permanently to the border.
imageAlt: Army Lasers Blast Cartel Drones Out of the Sky in Border Test
author: Michael Reynolds

title: Texas Guard's AH-64E Apaches Relocate to JBSA-Lackland in Army Reshuffle
summary: The Texas Guard's Apache attack battalion has begun moving to Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland under an Army restructuring plan.
content:
The Texas Army National Guard's AH-64E Apache battalion has begun relocating to Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, part of a broader Army plan to reformat its aviation forces.

The 1st Battalion, 149th Aviation Regiment — an attack reconnaissance battalion under the 36th Combat Aviation Brigade — started the move recently, according to the Defense Department.

The AH-64E Apache Guardian is the latest version of the Army's legendary attack helicopter, with improved sensors, networking, and the ability to control drones from the cockpit. Guard Apaches give states a potent capability for both federal missions and domestic emergencies.

The relocation is part of the Army's ongoing effort to consolidate aviation units at major installations, where maintenance, training ranges, and support infrastructure are concentrated.

The move is expected to take months to complete.
imageAlt: Texas Guard's AH-64E Apaches Relocate to JBSA-Lackland in Army Reshuffle
author: David Sullivan

title: Navy-Marine Osprey Test Opens New Anti-Submarine Chapter
summary: An MV-22B Osprey has dropped sonobuoys in its first lot acceptance test, paving the way for tiltrotor anti-submarine warfare.
content:
A joint Navy-Marine Corps team has executed the first lot acceptance test of sonobuoys dropped from an MV-22B Osprey tiltrotor off San Clemente Island, California — laying the groundwork for a new era of tiltrotor anti-submarine warfare.

The test, announced by the Defense Department, proved the Osprey can dispense the acoustic sensors that hunt submarines. Sonobuoys listen for undersea contacts and relay what they hear to aircraft overhead; until now, dropping them was the job of fixed-wing patrol planes and helicopters.

An ASW-capable Osprey would be a significant addition. The tiltrotor flies twice as fast and far as a helicopter, letting it sprint to a suspected submarine contact and then hover to prosecute it — combining the best of both worlds.

With Chinese and Russian submarine activity rising, the Navy is hungry for more ASW capacity across distributed forces.

The test clears the way for expanded tactical use of sonobuoys across the Osprey fleet.
imageAlt: Navy-Marine Osprey Test Opens New Anti-Submarine Chapter
author: Robert Hayes

title: Sea Drone That Rescued Downed Apache Crew Hailed by Pentagon Chief
summary: The Pentagon's civilian chief visited the Texas company whose unmanned surface vessel helped rescue a downed Apache crew.
content:
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth visited Saronic Technologies in Austin, Texas, to meet the team behind the unmanned surface vessel that helped rescue a downed Apache helicopter crew.

The visit, part of Hegseth's "Arsenal of Freedom" tour spotlighting the defense industrial base, highlighted a rescue that has become a signature story for military unmanned systems: a sea drone reaching crew members in distress where manned rescue might have been slower or riskier.

Saronic builds autonomous surface vessels designed for the Navy's hybrid fleet — small, attritable, and increasingly autonomous. The company's rise mirrors the Pentagon's broader bet that unmanned systems will multiply the fleet's reach without multiplying its cost.

The Apache rescue demonstrated the other side of that bet: drones not just as weapons, but as lifesavers.

Hegseth's tour has focused on companies outside the traditional defense primes, signaling where the Pentagon wants innovation to come from.
imageAlt: Sea Drone That Rescued Downed Apache Crew Hailed by Pentagon Chief
author: James Carter

title: U.S. Delivers $6 Million in Long-Range Drones to Panama for Border Security
summary: The U.S. has delivered four long-range K1000 drones worth over $6 million to Panama to fight smuggling and secure transit routes.
content:
The United States has delivered four long-range K1000 unmanned aircraft — valued at more than $6 million — to Panama's Ministry of Public Security, expanding security cooperation aimed at halting smuggling and transnational threats.

U.S. Ambassador Kevin Marino Cabrera handed over the drones, funded by U.S. Southern Command, with a clear stated purpose: stopping threats and illegal smuggling routes long before they approach the American homeland, according to the Defense Department.

The K1000 is a long-endurance unmanned system built for persistent surveillance over remote terrain — exactly the environment of Panama's Darien region, a notorious corridor for drug trafficking and migrant smuggling.

The delivery reflects Washington's strategy of pushing security outward: equipping partners to interdict threats at the source rather than at the U.S. border.

Panamanian forces will operate the aircraft with American training and support.
imageAlt: U.S. Delivers $6 Million in Long-Range Drones to Panama for Border Security
author: Michael Reynolds

title: USS George Washington Recovers Its 200,000th Aircraft in 34 Years at Sea
summary: After 34 years of service, the carrier USS George Washington has trapped its 200,000th fixed-wing aircraft — a milestone reached in the Indian Ocean.
content:
The aircraft carrier USS George Washington has recovered its 200,000th fixed-wing aircraft, a milestone reached while underway in the Indian Ocean after 34 years of continuous service.

Every "trap" — the controlled crash of a jet catching an arresting wire at 150 miles per hour — is a small feat of precision. Two hundred thousand of them represents decades of round-the-clock flight operations, from combat missions to humanitarian relief.

The George Washington, forward-deployed to Japan, is the Navy's only permanently forward-based carrier, putting it at the center of American power projection in the Indo-Pacific. It is currently supporting operations against Iran, the only carrier doing so after the USS George H.W. Bush stood down.

Nimitz-class carriers like the Washington are being succeeded by the Ford class, but with a service life measured in decades, the ship will remain a fleet mainstay for years.

The Navy did not identify the milestone aircraft or its squadron.
imageAlt: USS George Washington Recovers Its 200,000th Aircraft in 34 Years at Sea
author: David Sullivan

title: 'Red Tails' Train to Keep F-35s Flying Under Fire
summary: Alabama's 187th Fighter Wing — the famed Red Tails — drilled generating F-35 combat sorties under pressure during Operation Tuskegee Thunder.
content:
Airmen of the 187th Fighter Wing — the Alabama Air National Guard unit carrying the legendary "Red Tails" name — have been training to generate and sustain F-35A combat airpower under pressure during Operation Tuskegee Thunder at Dannelly Field.

The exercise drilled the unglamorous side of airpower: turning jets quickly, fixing them fast, and operating from austere locations while under simulated attack, according to the Defense Department. Modern air wars are won as much by maintainers and logisticians as by pilots.

The Red Tails name honors the Tuskegee Airmen, the Black fighter pilots of World War II whose escort record became legend. Today's 187th flies the F-35A Lightning II, the Air Force's stealth workhorse.

The focus on dispersed, resilient operations reflects hard lessons from Ukraine and the Pacific: concentrated airbases are targets, and the side that keeps flying after the first strike wins.

The wing regularly deploys worldwide in support of combatant commanders.
imageAlt: 'Red Tails' Train to Keep F-35s Flying Under Fire
author: Robert Hayes

title: Secretive AIM-260 Missile Spotted on Australian Super Hornet
summary: The long-range AIM-260 air-to-air missile has been photographed on an Australian F/A-18F Super Hornet, promising a major reach boost against Chinese threats.
content:
The secretive AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile has been photographed carried by an Australian F/A-18F Super Hornet — a rare public sighting of the weapon meant to replace the AMRAAM.

The photos, reported by The War Zone, show the long-range air-to-air missile on a Royal Australian Air Force jet. For Australia, the AIM-260 promises what its air force needs most: reach. Against Chinese fighters armed with very-long-range missiles, Australian Hornets and future aircraft have been outranged.

The AIM-260 has been in development for years under unusual secrecy, with the Air Force disclosing little about its range or capabilities. It is designed to outrange the AIM-120D AMRAAM it replaces, restoring the beyond-visual-range advantage.

Australia's access to the missile signals the depth of U.S.-Australian airpower integration under AUKUS-era cooperation.

Neither government has commented on delivery timelines.
imageAlt: Secretive AIM-260 Missile Spotted on Australian Super Hornet
author: James Carter

title: Ukraine's F-16 Fleet Faces Readiness Crisis as War Grinds On
summary: More than half of Ukraine's donated F-16s are reportedly grounded, and Western air-to-air missile stocks are running low.
content:
More than half of Ukraine's fleet of donated F-16 fighters is reportedly grounded, as the war grinds on and Western air-to-air missile stocks run low, according to The War Zone.

The readiness crisis threatens one of Ukraine's most important Western capabilities. The F-16s — donated by the Netherlands, Denmark, Norway, and Belgium — gave Kyiv its first modern fighters, used for air defense against Russian cruise missiles and drones.

But the jets are aging airframes, maintenance-intensive and dependent on a spare-parts pipeline that was never designed for wartime tempo. Keeping them flying requires constant Western support, and every grounded jet is one fewer interceptor against nightly Russian attacks.

Compounding the problem, stocks of Western air-to-air missiles are reportedly thinning — the same munitions the F-16s expend shooting down Shahed drones and cruise missiles.

Ukraine has asked partners for more jets, more parts, and more missiles. Whether the pipeline can keep pace is now an open question.
imageAlt: Ukraine's F-16 Fleet Faces Readiness Crisis as War Grinds On
author: Michael Reynolds

title: One Navy Squadron's Staggering Weapons Bill from the War with Iran
summary: A single Navy fighter squadron — VFA-41 — expended hundreds of air-to-air and air-to-surface weapons during Operation Epic Fury against Iran.
content:
Strike Fighter Squadron 41, the "Black Aces," expended hundreds of air-to-air and air-to-surface weapons during Operation Epic Fury — the war with Iran — according to a remarkable accounting reported by The War Zone.

The tally from a single F/A-18F Super Hornet squadron illustrates the sheer scale of the air campaign: hundreds of precision bombs, air-to-air missiles, and other munitions in weeks of combat. Multiply that across the carrier air wing, and the expenditure becomes staggering.

The numbers also highlight a strategic worry: munitions stockpiles. Precision weapons take years to build, and a short, intense war can burn through reserves faster than industry replaces them. Pentagon planners have been warning about exactly this.

VFA-41's Super Hornets flew strike and fighter missions from the carrier deck around the clock, a tempo that tested both the jets and their crews.

The full accounting offers a rare window into what modern naval air warfare actually costs in ordnance.
imageAlt: One Navy Squadron's Staggering Weapons Bill from the War with Iran
author: David Sullivan

title: Germany Finally Gives Its F125 Frigates Real Teeth with IRIS-T Missiles
summary: Germany is arming its 7,200-ton F125 frigates with IRIS-T SLM surface-to-air missiles, addressing their notoriously light armament.
content:
Germany is finally giving its F125 frigates some real firepower, fitting the 7,200-ton warships with IRIS-T SLM surface-to-air missiles.

The F125s were built with notoriously light armament for ships their size — a design choice that drew years of criticism, The War Zone reports. Adding IRIS-T SLM, a capable medium-range air defense missile, partly addresses the gap.

IRIS-T SLM is the surface-launched version of the IRIS-T air-to-air missile, with a vertical-launch variant offering 360-degree engagement against aircraft, cruise missiles, and drones. It has seen combat in Ukraine, where German-supplied systems have performed well against Russian air attacks.

The upgrade reflects Germany's broader naval rearmament. After decades of underinvestment, Berlin is now spending heavily on its fleet — new frigates, submarines, and missile upgrades across the board.

For the F125s, designed for stabilization missions rather than high-end combat, the missiles are a step toward credibility in contested waters.

Installation timelines have not been disclosed.
imageAlt: Germany Finally Gives Its F125 Frigates Real Teeth with IRIS-T Missiles
author: Robert Hayes
